curated_by: Owner-approved curation, drafted by Claude (Claude Code); each reading names a published proponent. Owner review pending.
note: Curated, sourced readings (not AI). Options are equal and unranked. Spans: end 0 = last verse of the chapter.

options.label: Framework: the days as a literary pattern
options.detail: Meredith Kline reads the six days as a literary framework (two matching sets of three days), arranging creation by theme rather than giving a chronological sequence.

options.label: Creation story drawing on ancient myth
options.detail: Hermann Gunkel argued that Genesis 1 reworks older Near Eastern creation myths, especially the image of God mastering the waters of chaos.

options.label: History of real events
options.detail: James Hoffmeier argues that Genesis 1–11 presents itself as history and is meant to be read as an account of real events, told with theological purpose.

options.label: Protohistory: real events told in a figurative way
options.detail: Gordon Wenham calls Genesis 1–11 “protohistory”: it refers to real people and events but tells them in a stylised, symbolic way to explain humanity’s condition.

options.label: Ancient-style history, not history in our sense
options.detail: Kenton Sparks argues that Genesis 1–11 is ancient historiography that uses traditional stories, so it should not be read as accurate modern history.

options.label: Founding legends of Israel and humanity
options.detail: Hermann Gunkel read Genesis as a collection of legends (Sagen): traditional stories that explain origins, names and customs.

options.label: Adam and Eve: the first couple, ancestors of all
options.detail: William Barrick holds that Adam and Eve were a real, specially created first pair, the sole ancestors of all people, living a few thousand years ago.

options.label: Adam and Eve: a real couple heading humanity
options.detail: C. John Collins argues that Adam and Eve were real people at the headwaters of humanity, possibly as leaders of a wider early population.

options.label: Adam and Eve as archetypes of all humanity
options.detail: John Walton reads Adam and Eve mainly as archetypes: the text uses them to represent every human being. He thinks they may also have been real people, but that is not the text’s main point.

options.label: Israel’s story told through Adam
options.detail: Peter Enns reads the Adam story as a portrait of Israel in miniature: placed in a good land, given a command, disobeying and being exiled.

options.label: Not a historical couple: an ancient picture of origins
options.detail: Denis Lamoureux holds that Adam never existed: the story uses the ancient science of its time to teach spiritual truths about God and sin.

options.label: Genealogical Adam: a real couple, ancestors of all by descent
options.detail: Joshua Swamidass argues that a recently created Adam and Eve could be genealogical ancestors of everyone alive by about AD 1, alongside an evolving wider population.
